unit.title: Perform weld in the flat and horizontal positions using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which filter shade is suggested for a welding helmet when welding with a 3.2 mm electrode at about 100–125 amps?
options: Shade 3
Shade 5
Shade 10
Shade 14

questions.stem: Why must the welding area be well ventilated?
options: To carry fumes and gases away from the welder's breathing zone
To keep the electrodes dry and stop the flux from taking in water
To cool the work piece faster so that it does not distort
To make the arc easier to strike and hold at a steady length

questions.stem: Which clothing is the safest to wear when arc welding?
options: A short-sleeved cotton T-shirt with a leather apron over it
A long-sleeved polyester or nylon shirt, buttoned up
A loose vest and shorts, to stay cool in the heat
A long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather jacket

questions.stem: What is the safe way to change an electrode?
options: Take off your gloves first so that you can grip the new electrode firmly
Wear dry gloves and keep the holder clear of the work and your body
Dip the holder in water first so that it is cool to handle
Touch the electrode on the work first to check that it is live

questions.stem: What is the main extra danger of arc welding in wet conditions?
options: The electrode burns more slowly
A higher risk of electric shock
The slag becomes harder to remove
The arc becomes brighter

questions.stem: What causes "arc eye" (arc flash burns to the eyes)?
options: Breathing welding fumes for too long without wearing a mask
Hot slag or spatter touching the skin of the face
Welding at too low an amperage for the electrode
Ultraviolet light from the arc reaching unprotected eyes

questions.stem: What protects your eyes when you chip slag from a weld?
options: Clear safety glasses or a clear face shield
Nothing — eye protection is only needed while welding
Sunglasses
Closing your eyes while chipping

questions.stem: Which fire precaution should be taken before welding starts?
options: Keep oily rags near the job to wipe the plates
Keep the fire extinguisher locked in the office
Remove anything that can burn and keep an extinguisher close by
Weld next to stored paper so that it can be used to cover the hot job

questions.stem: In shielded metal arc welding, which part holds the electrode and carries the current to it?
options: The work clamp
The chipping hammer
The fillet gauge
The electrode holder

questions.stem: Where should the work lead (return) clamp be connected?
options: To a water pipe or steel beam anywhere in the building
To the work piece or welding table, close to the weld
To the electrode holder, so that the circuit is complete
To the metal frame of the welding machine itself

questions.stem: What should be done with a welding cable whose insulation is damaged?
options: Wrap the damaged part in masking tape and carry on
Carry on, but only at low amperage until the job is done
Have it repaired properly or replaced before it is used
Keep the cable wet so that the damaged part stays cool

questions.stem: What kind of welding current does a basic transformer welding machine (with no rectifier) supply?
options: Alternating current (AC)
Direct current (DC) only
No current until a gas cylinder is connected
Three-phase direct current

questions.stem: What does DCEP (direct current electrode positive) mean?
options: The electrode holder lead is connected to the positive terminal
The work lead is connected to the positive terminal of the machine
The machine supplies alternating current
The machine is switched off

questions.stem: Within an electrode's working range, what does raising the welding current generally do?
options: Reduces penetration
Stops the electrode from melting
Increases penetration and makes the electrode melt faster
Makes the slag thicker but changes nothing else about the weld

questions.stem: In the electrode classification E6013, what does the letter "E" stand for?
options: Every position
Electrode
Easy strike
Extra iron powder

questions.stem: In the classification E6013, what does "60" tell you?
options: The electrode is 60 mm long, not counting the bare grip end
The highest welding current to use is 60 amps
The flux coating makes up 60 per cent of its weight
The weld metal's minimum tensile strength is 60 000 psi

questions.stem: In the classification E6013, what does the third digit, "1", tell you?
options: The electrode can be used in the flat position only
The electrode can be used for flat and horizontal fillets only
The electrode can be used in all positions
The electrode is for cutting only

questions.stem: What is the main job of the flux coating on a shielded metal arc electrode?
options: To insulate the electrode so that the welder cannot get an electric shock
To make the electrode stiffer so that it does not bend
To give the electrode a clean look and stop it rusting
To shield the molten metal from the air and form a protective slag

questions.stem: How should low-hydrogen electrodes such as E7018 be kept once the packet is opened?
options: Dry, in a heated electrode oven
Soaked in water before use
Outdoors, in the open air
Wrapped in a damp cloth

questions.stem: What should you do with an electrode whose coating is damp or cracked?
options: Use it anyway, at a higher amperage
Set it aside and do not use it for the job
Knock off the loose coating and use it
Use it only for the root pass, where it is hidden

questions.stem: An electrode is sold as "3.2 mm". What does the 3.2 mm measure?
options: The thickness of the flux coating
The diameter of the metal core wire
The length of the electrode
The width of the bead it makes

questions.stem: Why must mill scale, rust, oil and paint be removed from the plate before welding?
options: They can cause porosity and poor fusion
They make the plate too heavy to position
They would make the finished weld too strong
They stop spatter from sticking to the plate

questions.stem: What is the usual included angle of a single-V butt joint on 10 mm plate?
options: About 15°
About 120°
About 180°
About 60°

questions.stem: On a bevelled plate edge, what is the "root face" (land)?
options: The top surface of the plate next to the bevel
The flat face of the electrode holder's jaws
The small flat left at the bottom of the bevel
The width of the finished weld at its face

questions.stem: What are tack welds for?
options: To finish the joint quickly without a full weld
To test the welding machine before the job starts
To mark the plate where it will be cut later
To hold the parts in line before the full weld is made

questions.stem: Which of these helps to reduce distortion when welding plate?
options: Using the largest electrode at the highest current
Welding without any tack welds, so that the plates can move freely
Tacking and clamping well and welding in a balanced sequence
Cooling the hot weld in water straight away

questions.stem: For a fillet weld in the horizontal position (2F), how should the electrode be pointed into the joint?
options: At 90° to the vertical plate, pointing straight at it
At about 45° between the plates, aimed a bit more at the bottom plate
Parallel to the joint, laid along the line of the weld
At about 10° to the top plate, aimed at the vertical face of the joint

questions.stem: Which travel angle is normally used for shielded metal arc welding in the flat position?
options: A drag angle of about 10° to 20°
A push angle of about 70°
The electrode laid flat on the plate
Any angle — it makes no difference

questions.stem: For most shielded metal arc electrodes, how long should the arc be?
options: About the same as the diameter of the electrode's core wire
About ten times the electrode diameter
No gap at all, with the electrode touching the plate the whole time
About 25 mm

questions.stem: What does too long an arc usually cause?
options: Deeper penetration with no spatter
The electrode sticking to the plate
A perfectly smooth bead
Spatter, porosity and a wide, uneven bead

questions.stem: The electrode sticks to the plate as you strike the arc. What should you do?
options: Pull it straight up as hard as you can while the arc is still burning
Leave it in place until it burns through by itself
Twist it free; if it stays stuck, release it from the holder first
Knock it off with the edge of your welding helmet

questions.stem: What does travelling too fast usually produce?
options: A wide, flat bead with too much weld metal piled up on the plate
A narrow, high bead with poor fusion and possible undercut
Burn-through on every pass, even on thick plate
Deeper penetration and a smoother, flatter bead

questions.stem: How should you restart a bead after changing the electrode?
options: Strike the arc on top of the old slag and carry straight on
Grind away all of the bead already welded and start the joint again
Clean the crater, strike just ahead of it, then move back into it
Change to a larger electrode and start at the far end

questions.stem: Why must a multi-pass weld be cleaned between passes?
options: So that the weld cools faster before the next pass
So that slag is not trapped under the next pass
To remove the tack welds before the cap is laid
Only so that the finished weld looks polished

questions.stem: What does the position code "1F" mean?
options: A groove weld in the vertical position
A fillet weld made overhead
A weld on pipe
A fillet weld in the flat position

questions.stem: What does the position code "2G" mean?
options: A groove weld in the horizontal position
A fillet weld in the flat position
A groove weld made overhead
A groove weld made vertical-up

questions.stem: When welding in the horizontal position, what does the molten pool tend to do?
options: Run uphill
Sag towards the lower plate because of gravity
Stay in place whatever the electrode angle
Freeze before the arc reaches it

questions.stem: What is undercut?
options: Slag trapped inside the weld between two passes
Small gas holes in the face of the weld metal
A groove melted along the toe of the weld and left unfilled
Too much weld metal built up on the face of the weld

questions.stem: Which of these is a common cause of porosity in a shielded metal arc weld?
options: Damp electrodes, dirty plate or too long an arc
Holding a short, steady arc of the correct length
Using clean, dry electrodes from the oven
Cleaning the plate to bright metal before welding

questions.stem: What most often causes slag inclusions?
options: Wearing a welding helmet with too dark a shade
Having too much ventilation in the welding booth
Cleaning the plate to bright metal before welding
Not cleaning the slag off fully between passes

questions.stem: What does "lack of fusion" mean?
options: The finished weld is much wider than the drawing allows it to be
The electrode coating was too dry when it was used
The face of the bead shows even ripples along it
The weld metal has not melted into the plate or the pass before

questions.stem: What is arc blow?
options: The arc pushed off line by magnetic forces, mostly with DC
The flux coating cracking and falling off the electrode
Wind blowing the flame out on an oxy-fuel torch
The helmet's filter lens cracking from the heat

questions.stem: What is a fillet weld gauge used to check?
options: The current the welding machine is set to
The hardness of the electrode's flux coating
The size of a fillet weld (its leg length and throat)
The flow rate of shielding gas at the torch

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a good fillet weld on a 2F test piece?
options: A tall, narrow bead sitting high on top of the plates
Equal legs, even ripples, smooth blending and no undercut
A thin layer of slag left on to protect the bead
Small holes on the face where the gas escaped

questions.stem: What should be done with electrode stubs at the end of a job?
options: Put them in a metal container kept for stubs
Leave them on the floor until they have cooled
Throw them in the waste bin with the paper
Throw them outside the workshop door

essays.stem: Describe the personal protective equipment a welder must wear for shielded metal arc welding, and say what each item protects against.
essays.modelAnswer: A welding helmet with the right filter shade (about shade 10 for a 3.2 mm electrode at 100–125 A) protects the eyes and face from ultraviolet and infrared light and from spatter. Clear safety glasses under the helmet protect the eyes when the helmet is lifted to chip slag or grind. Dry leather welding gauntlets protect the hands from heat, spatter and electric shock. A long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather jacket (or leather apron and sleeves), worn buttoned up, protects the skin from arc radiation, sparks and spatter. Safety boots protect the feet from falling plate and hot metal, with trousers worn over the boots so spatter cannot fall in. Ear protection is worn when grinding or in a noisy workshop, and a respirator where ventilation cannot keep fumes away.
markingPoints: Helmet with the correct filter shade — protects eyes and face from arc radiation and spatter
Clear safety glasses for chipping and grinding
Dry leather gloves — heat, spatter and electric shock
Flame-resistant long-sleeved jacket or leather apron — burns and arc radiation
Safety boots, with trousers over them — falling objects and spatter (ear protection or respirator as needed)

essays.stem: Explain how you would prepare and set up two pieces of 10 mm carbon steel plate for a single-V butt weld in the flat position.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the drawing and check the plate size. Cut the plates and bevel each edge to about 30° by grinding or flame cutting, giving an included angle of about 60°. Grind a root face of about 2–3 mm on each edge. Clean the bevels and about 25 mm each side back to bright metal, removing mill scale, rust, oil and paint. Lay the plates flat with a root gap of about 2.5–3 mm (a spacer or an electrode can be used to set it), check that they are level and in line, and tack each end on the back or inside the joint. Set a slight pre-set (a small angle) so that the plates pull flat as the weld shrinks. Clean the tacks and check the gap again before welding.
markingPoints: Bevel each edge about 30° (60° included)
Root face of about 2–3 mm
Clean back to bright metal, about 25 mm each side
Set the root gap (about 2.5–3 mm) and align the plates
Tack the ends and allow a pre-set against distortion

essays.stem: Explain how arc length, amperage and travel speed each affect the quality of a shielded metal arc bead.
essays.modelAnswer: Arc length: the arc should be about the diameter of the core wire. Too long an arc gives spatter, porosity, a wide uneven bead and poor shielding; too short an arc makes the electrode stick and the bead high and narrow. Amperage: within the maker's range, more current gives deeper penetration and a wider, flatter bead; too much causes undercut, spatter and burn-through, and too little gives poor fusion, a high narrow bead and a hard-to-hold arc. Travel speed: too fast gives a narrow, thin bead with poor fusion and undercut; too slow gives a wide, heavy bead, too much heat, and risks slag running ahead and being trapped. The right combination gives an even bead with good fusion into both edges.
markingPoints: Correct arc length about one core-wire diameter; too long = spatter and porosity
Too short an arc = sticking and a high narrow bead
Higher amperage = more penetration; too high = undercut or burn-through
Too low amperage = poor fusion and a high narrow bead
Travel speed: too fast = narrow bead and poor fusion; too slow = heavy bead and slag trapped

essays.stem: Describe how to strike and keep an arc with an E6013 electrode, and how to restart a bead after changing the electrode.
essays.modelAnswer: With PPE on and the helmet down, strike the arc by scratching the electrode tip lightly on the plate, like striking a match, or by tapping it, then lift it quickly to the correct arc length (about the core-wire diameter). Hold a steady drag angle of about 10°–20° and feed the electrode down as it burns so that the arc length stays the same, travelling at an even speed while watching the pool. If the electrode sticks, free it with a quick twist or release it from the holder. To restart, chip the slag from the crater and brush it, strike the arc about 10–15 mm ahead of the crater, move back into the crater to fill it, then carry on along the joint so that the join is smooth with no gap or lump.
markingPoints: Scratch or tap start, then lift to the correct arc length
Steady drag angle and electrode fed down to keep the arc length
Even travel speed, watching the pool
Clean the slag from the crater before restarting
Strike just ahead of the crater, move back to fill it, then continue

essays.stem: Explain how to make a three-pass fillet weld in the horizontal position (2F) on a tee joint of 10 mm plate, including the electrode angles and the order of the passes.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean and tack the plates square to make a tee joint, with no gap at the root. Set the current for the electrode (for example 3.2 mm E6013 within the maker's range). Pass 1 (root): point the electrode at about 45° into the root, slightly towards the bottom plate, with a drag angle of about 10°–20°, and fuse into both plates. Chip and brush the slag. Pass 2: lay a bead along the bottom plate, overlapping about half of the root pass, with the electrode angled slightly more down towards the bottom plate. Clean again. Pass 3: lay a bead along the top, overlapping pass 2 and fusing into the vertical plate, with the electrode angled slightly up so that the metal does not sag. Clean the slag and check that the legs are equal and to size with no undercut on the vertical plate.
markingPoints: Tee joint cleaned, tacked square, no root gap
Root pass at about 45° work angle with a 10°–20° drag angle
Slag removed between every pass
Second pass on the bottom plate, third pass on the top, each overlapping
Finished legs equal and to size, no undercut on the vertical plate

essays.stem: Name four common defects in shielded metal arc welds. For each, give one cause and one way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Porosity — caused by damp electrodes, dirty plate or too long an arc; prevented by dry electrodes, clean plate and the correct arc length. Slag inclusion — caused by not cleaning between passes or a wrong electrode angle; prevented by chipping and brushing every pass and keeping the right angle. Undercut — caused by too much current, too long an arc or the wrong angle; prevented by correct current, arc length and angle and a short pause at the edges. Lack of fusion — caused by too little current, too fast travel or a dirty joint; prevented by the right current and speed and a clean joint. Cracks (or incomplete penetration) — caused by fast cooling or a root gap that is too small; prevented by the right preparation, gap and procedure.
markingPoints: Four defects named correctly (for example porosity, slag inclusion, undercut, lack of fusion, cracks, incomplete penetration)
A correct cause for each
A correct way to prevent each
Links each defect to current, arc length, speed, cleaning or preparation
Clear and in full sentences

essays.stem: Explain why electrodes must be stored correctly, and describe how E7018 low-hydrogen electrodes should be stored and handled.
essays.modelAnswer: An electrode's flux coating soaks up moisture from the air. Damp electrodes give porosity, spatter and an unstable arc, and with low-hydrogen electrodes the moisture brings hydrogen into the weld, which can cause cracking. A damaged coating gives poor shielding. E7018 electrodes are kept sealed until needed; once a packet is opened they are kept in a heated electrode oven at the temperature the maker gives, and taken out only as needed (in a portable heated quiver if possible). Electrodes left out longer than the maker allows, or that have got wet, are re-dried exactly as the maker says or not used. They are handled with clean, dry gloves and not bent or dropped.
markingPoints: Coatings absorb moisture from the air
Damp electrodes cause porosity, spatter and an unstable arc
Low-hydrogen: moisture adds hydrogen, which can cause cracking
E7018 kept sealed, then in a heated electrode oven once opened
Handled dry; damp or damaged electrodes re-dried as the maker says or not used

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make on the welding machine, cables, electrode holder and work clamp before starting work, and say why each check matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that the machine is switched off and properly connected to the supply, with its casing undamaged and its own earth connected, so that it is safe to touch. Check the welding cables along their whole length for cuts, burns or bare wire, and that every connection is tight, because damaged insulation or loose joints can give an electric shock, overheat or cause a fire. Check that the electrode holder's insulation is not cracked or burnt and that its jaws grip properly, and that the work clamp is clean, grips firmly and is fixed close to the weld, so that the current returns safely and the arc is steady. Check that the area is dry and clear of anything that can burn, with screens in place. Faults are reported and the equipment is not used until repaired.
markingPoints: Machine off, correctly connected, casing and earth sound
Cables checked along their length for damage; connections tight
Electrode holder insulation and jaws in good condition
Work clamp clean and fixed close to the weld
Reasons given (shock, overheating, fire, steady arc); faults reported and not used

essays.stem: Explain what causes distortion when welding plate, and describe three ways to control it.
essays.modelAnswer: The weld and the metal beside it are heated and expand, then contract as they cool. Because the heating is uneven, the shrinking pulls the plate out of shape: a butt joint closes up and bends, and a tee joint pulls the upright plate over. Distortion can be controlled by: tacking well and clamping or using a jig so the parts cannot move; presetting the parts at a small angle so that the shrinking pulls them straight; welding in a balanced sequence (alternating sides or back-step welding) so that the forces cancel; using no more weld metal and heat than needed (the right size of weld and number of passes); and letting the work cool naturally rather than quenching it.
markingPoints: Heating and cooling — expansion then contraction — pulls the plate out of shape
Clamping, jigs and good tacks
Presetting the parts to allow for shrinkage
A balanced welding sequence or back-step welding
Not over-welding; letting the work cool naturally

essays.stem: Describe how you would visually inspect a completed fillet weld, and what you would look for.
essays.modelAnswer: Let the weld cool, then chip off all the slag and wire-brush it. Look at the weld in good light along its whole length. Check its size with a fillet weld gauge: the legs should be equal and to the size on the drawing, with the right throat. Check the profile: a flat or slightly convex face, with even ripples and width. Look for surface defects: undercut at the toes, overlap, porosity (holes), cracks, slag left on the surface, and craters not filled at the ends. Check that the weld blends smoothly into both plates and that the plates are square and not distorted. Note anything that does not meet the standard and report it.
markingPoints: Slag removed and the weld cleaned before inspecting
Size checked with a fillet gauge — equal legs to drawing
Profile and even ripples checked
Defects looked for: undercut, overlap, porosity, cracks, unfilled craters
Squareness or distortion checked; faults recorded and reported

practical1.title: Three-pass fillet weld in the horizontal position (2F) on a tee joint
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a safe welding station and weld a tee joint in 10 mm carbon steel plate (two pieces, about 150 mm × 75 mm) with a three-pass fillet weld in the horizontal position (2F), using 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes. Every member makes at least one pass while the assessor watches, cleans the slag before the next pass, and takes part in checking the finished weld with a fillet gauge. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the weld is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 2 pieces of 10 mm carbon steel plate, about 150 mm × 75 mm
photos: The welding station set up, with every member in full PPE
Plates cleaned and tacked square as a tee joint
Finished three-pass fillet weld — top view
Finished weld — end view, showing both legs
The fillet gauge on the finished weld
The work area cleaned, stubs in a metal container
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout (helmet with a suitable shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket, boots)
Checked the machine, cables, electrode holder and work clamp before welding
Set the current within the maker's range for 3.2 mm E6013
Cleaned the plates and tacked them square and in line
Held a steady arc of the right length, with the correct work and travel angles
Removed the slag fully between passes
Finished fillet: equal legs to size, no undercut, porosity or slag on the surface
Left the work area safe and tidy, with stubs in a metal container
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens so others are not exposed to arc flash
Remove anything that can burn; keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Keep gloves and clothing dry; never stand in water
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
Make sure the area is ventilated; keep your head out of the fumes

practical2.title: Single-V butt weld in the flat position (1G) on 10 mm plate
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare and weld a single-V butt joint in two pieces of 10 mm carbon steel plate (about 150 mm × 100 mm) in the flat position (1G). Bevel each edge to about 30° (60° included), with a root face of about 2–3 mm, set a root gap of about 2.5–3 mm and tack with a slight pre-set. Weld a root pass, then fill and cap with 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes, cleaning between passes. Every member makes at least one pass while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the weld is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 2 pieces of 10 mm carbon steel plate, about 150 mm × 100 mm
photos: Bevelled edges, showing the root face
Plates tacked with the root gap and pre-set
Root pass from the top, cleaned
Back of the joint, showing the penetration
The work area cleaned, stubs in a metal container
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout, including eye protection when grinding
Bevelled the edges to about 30° with a root face of about 2–3 mm
Set the root gap and tacked the plates in line with a pre-set
Made a root pass with even penetration on the back
Removed the slag fully between passes
Capping pass of even width and height, with no undercut
No porosity, cracks or slag visible on the face
Left the work area safe and tidy, with stubs in a metal container
safety: Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding; check the disc is right for the grinder and undamaged
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before striking an arc
Remove anything that can burn; keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Keep gloves and clothing dry; never stand in water
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
